transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Hurst.
Tens of millions of people along the east coast are in the path of a major nor'easter.
The storm's already disrupted sports games, flights and concerts.
Now strong winds and heavy rain are moving into the region, causing flooding as it parks
itself off the coast.
And here's Amy Held has more.
An unusually early season nor'easter is upending the weekend from the Carolinas to New England.
On Long Island in New York, Melissa Slavin says she's ready for 48 hours inside with
her kids.
"Buy extra groceries, preparing, rescheduling all the kids' sports."
Coastal flooding is forecast to be significant widespread and repeated.
At the Jersey Shore...
"Take this storm seriously."
Mike Mangan is mayor of Manasquan.
"There's going to be a lot of water in the streets for a long time."
Part of the problem?
The system is lingering, says meteorologist Frank Pereira.
"It's going to kind of sit there for a day or two through the remainder of the weekend,
kind of looping around that area before it finally moves out early next week."
Tonight's moon is full, making for even higher tides and flooding.
Amy Held, NPR News.
President Trump heads to Tennessee today for a college football matchup, but CNN won't
be on Air Force One.
The White House barred them from the ride, the latest media restrictions amid an ongoing
First Amendment dispute.
Jackie Seiber of member station WUOT has more on the game.
Trump's presence comes as the University of Tennessee's campus is already teaming with
activity for ESPN's College Game Day show.
Student Cooper Dabbs participated in festivities hosted by ESPN.
"It's just going to be a great environment.
I think we have a good shot at winning if the fans help out."
Student Amber Henderson looks forward to the game, but has reservations.
"I don't think that the game is about football anymore.
I think it's more so about politics."
Fans are expected to see heightened security as they enter the stadium.
For NPR News, I'm Jackie Seiber in Knoxville.
OpenAI says its models probed government websites on their own.
NPR's Shannon Bond reports it's the latest episode where AI systems have gone rogue doing
things their developers didn't expect or asked them to do.
OpenAI's AI models tried to hack an Education Department website but were unsuccessful, according
to AI research firm Transloose.
The Education Department said it found no evidence of any impact, and OpenAI says it's
reviewing the researcher's findings.
OpenAI has notified dozens of organizations about times its AI acted in what it calls
misaligned ways during training and evaluation.
That includes accessing publicly available Census Bureau data using login keys found
online and copying public information from the Securities and Exchange Commission and
posting it to another website.
The SEC says no non-public information was accessed.
The Census Bureau didn't respond to a request for comment.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Russian attacks on Ukraine today left at least eight people dead as Moscow hammered Kiev with
crews and ballistic missiles, drones and glide bombs, this some four and a half years after
Russia started the war that shows no signs of ending.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's long-range drones targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses, sparking
a fire and killing at least three people.
In Brazil, with just a little over a week before national elections, the president has
ordered a ban on online betting.
The move, the Brazilian leader says, is for the health and welfare of families who are
falling deeper into debt in the South American country.
And here's Carrie Khan has more.
Online gambling has exploded in Brazil in recent years, and so has personal debt, as
well as gambling addictions and suicides, according to a recent national study.
In signing the banning order, President Luis Anacio Lula da Silva said his decision was
hard and drastic but necessary.
Lula is locked in a tough reelection campaign with the son of former right-wing President
Jair Bolsonaro.
Flavio Bolsonaro, who is polling at a statistical tie with Lula for the presidency, criticized
the ban as a, quote, "electoral measure."
Brazil's central bank estimates that Brazilians spend nearly $6 billion a month on gambling.
Brazil's soccer clubs, however, say without the advertising from online betting houses,
their clubs could close.
Carrie Khan, NPR News, Rio de Janeiro.
Investors on Wall Street this week bought bonds and dumped stocks.
This is the 10-year Treasury bond rose to its highest level in two decades.
This is NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's Vital Journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Major nor'easter impacts east coast from Carolinas to New England with flooding and disruptions
President Trump heads to Tennessee for college football game as CNN barred from Air Force One
OpenAI says its AI models probed U.S. government websites during training and evaluation
Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least eight people with missiles, drones and glide bombs
Ukraine targets Russian oil refineries with long-range drones, killing at least three people
Brazil President Lula orders ban on online betting citing debt and addiction concerns
Wall Street investors sell stocks and buy bonds as Treasury yields hit two-decade highs
